articles.title: ID Logistics and Terra Robotics plan humanoid robot pilot in Germany
articles.summary: ID Logistics has partnered with Terra Robotics to explore the use of humanoid robots in warehouse operations, with plans to launch its first pilot under real operating conditions in Germany within six months. articles.body: ID Logistics has partnered with Terra Robotics to explore the use of humanoid robots in warehouse operations, with plans to launch its first pilot under real operating conditions in Germany within six months. The strategic partnership, which took effect on 1 November 2026, follows initial tests involving two humanoid robots at facilities in Griesheim and Löhne. The companies aim to identify tasks where humanoid robots could support warehouse operations. Their focus includes sorting, order picking, packing and other repetitive logistics activities. The agreement also marks a further step in ID Logistics’ efforts to assess new automation technologies across its contract logistics operations. Two humanoid robots complete initial sorting tests ID Logistics and Terra Robotics began working together approximately one year ago. Each company invested in a Unitree G1 EDU6 humanoid robot to develop and test an initial sorting process. The robot named IDA is based at ID Logistics’ facility in Griesheim. Meanwhile, a second robot, named Heinz, is located at Terra Robotics in Löhne. Both robots were programmed to perform the same sorting task. They can now distinguish cardboard boxes from mailer bags and place them into shipping boxes. The robots use five-fingered hands equipped with tactile sensors to handle the different types of packaging. Robin Otto, CEO of ID Logistics Germany, said the logistics sector offers considerable potential for humanoid robotics because many warehouse processes involve repetitive tasks. The company intends to identify suitable applications and assess their performance in real operating environments before considering wider deployment. First operational pilot planned within six months The next phase will focus on selecting a suitable application for testing at an ID Logistics facility in Germany. Over the coming weeks, the partners will evaluate four or five potential use cases and define their technical and operational requirements. They will then select the most suitable task and robot model for the pilot. Terra Robotics’ portfolio includes humanoid robots from manufacturers such as Unitree and UBTECH. However, the companies have not yet confirmed which model will be used. The first pilot is scheduled to take place within six months of the announcement. It will assess the technology’s capabilities and limitations under real warehouse operating conditions. The results will help determine whether humanoid robots could support more complex logistics processes in the future. ID Logistics operates approximately 450 logistics facilities worldwide, including 17 in Germany. Its activities cover retail, e-commerce, consumer goods and other sectors. For now, the partnership remains focused on testing and evaluating the technology rather than deploying humanoid robots across the company’s wider logistics network.

articles.title: Vard Kicks Off Construction of UPO Atlantic CSOV
articles.summary: Vard has started construction of the UPO Atlantic commissioning service operation vessel (CSOV) for U-Ming Purus Offshore (UPO), following a steel-cutting ceremony at its Vard Vung Tau shipyard in Vietnam.The ceremony, held on November 2, marked the first construction milestone for the vessel…
articles.body: Vard Kicks Off Construction of UPO Atlantic CSOV Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 (Credit: Vard) Vard has started construction of the UPO Atlantic commissioning service operation vessel (CSOV) for U-Ming Purus Offshore (UPO), following a steel-cutting ceremony at its Vard Vung Tau shipyard in Vietnam. The ceremony, held on November 2, marked the first construction milestone for the vessel, designated NB 1004 and based on Vard's VARD 4 19 design. The UPO Atlantic is being developed to support offshore wind projects in Taiwan and across Asia, as part of UPO's expansion into the region's offshore wind market. UPO was established in October 2025 as a joint venture between U-Ming Marine Offshore (UMO) and Purus, with plans to commission two VARD 4 19 CSOVs designed for operating conditions in Taiwan. (Credit: UPO) The two vessels, each measuring 88 meters in length, will feature Seaonics all-electric Walk-to-Work (W2W) 3D gangways, enhanced DP2 dynamic positioning and hybrid propulsion systems designed to reduce emissions and improve fuel efficiency. Each CSOV will provide accommodation for up to 120 personnel, including up to 93 technicians, supporting long-duration offshore wind operations. Deliveries under the two-vessel program are scheduled to begin in 2027. UPO said the vessels will support offshore wind development in Taiwan and the wider Asia-Pacific region, with the UPO Atlantic intended for work associated with the construction and maintenance of offshore wind projects.

articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd unveils standalone AMX and ASX services linking Asia and Latin America
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has announced two standalone container shipping services connecting Asia with Latin America, as the German carrier prepares to expand its network in 2027. The new AMX and ASX services will provide connections to Mexico and the East Coast of South America, respectively. Both will operate independently...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd has announced two standalone container shipping services connecting Asia with Latin America, as the German carrier prepares to expand its network in 2027. The new AMX and ASX services will provide connections to Mexico and the East Coast of South America, respectively. Both will operate independently under Hapag-Lloyd’s network. According to the carrier, the changes aim to improve regional connectivity and provide customers with additional routing options. The AMX service is scheduled to begin in January 2027, while ASX will follow in April. AMX to connect Asia and Mexico from January The new AMX service will offer weekly sailings between Asia and Mexico, with direct calls in China, South Korea and three Mexican ports. The planned port rotation is: Ningbo – Qingdao – Busan – Ensenada – Manzanillo – Lázaro Cárdenas. Through transshipment connections in Mexico, customers will also gain access to additional destinations along the West Coast of Latin America. Hapag-Lloyd said the standalone structure will provide greater operational control over the service. Meanwhile, regular weekly departures will support cargo planning across the trade corridor. Detailed vessel schedules are expected to become available closer to the launch. ASX to strengthen Asia–South America connections The second service, ASX, will connect Asia with the East Coast of South America from April 2027. Its planned rotation includes direct calls at major Asian and Brazilian ports: Qingdao – Ningbo – Shekou – Tanjung Pelepas – Santos – Itajaí – Rio Grande – Paranaguá – Santos – Singapore – Qingdao. In addition, feeder services via Rio Grande will provide connections to Montevideo in Uruguay and Buenos Aires in Argentina. Both AMX and ASX will include direct calls at Qingdao, strengthening the carrier’s connections between northern China and Latin American markets. The ASX announcement comes as Hapag-Lloyd prepares to leave its existing vessel-sharing arrangement with MSC and Ocean Network Express (ONE) on the Asia–East Coast South America trade. MSC and ONE previously announced plans to continue their Ipanema/SX1 service without Hapag-Lloyd from April 2027. However, Hapag-Lloyd has not explicitly described ASX as a replacement for its existing AS2 service. The company has also not disclosed the number of vessels, deployed capacity or first sailing dates for the new standalone services. Further operational details are expected as Hapag-Lloyd prepares for their introduction in 2027.
takeaways: Hapag-Lloyd has announced two standalone container shipping services connecting Asia with Latin America, as the German carrier prepares to expand its network in 2027.
The new AMX and ASX services will provide connections to Mexico and the East Coast of South America, respectively.
Both will operate independently under Hapag-Lloyd’s network.

articles.title: Woodside to cut more than 500 jobs in $400m savings drive
articles.summary: Australian energy giant Woodside is planning to cut more than 500 jobs worldwide as part of a restructuring programme aimed at delivering $400m in annual cost savings from 2028. The workforce reduction, equivalent to more than 10% of the company’s employees at the end of 2025, forms part of a broader effort to...
articles.body: Offshore Woodside to cut more than 500 jobs in $400m savings drive Bojan Lepic November 5, 2026 0 95 1 minute read Woodside Woodside Australian energy giant Woodside is planning to cut more than 500 jobs worldwide as part of a restructuring programme aimed at delivering $400m in annual cost savings from 2028. The workforce reduction, equivalent to more than 10% of the company’s employees at the end of 2025, forms part of a broader effort to streamline operations, reduce external spending and reshape its oil and gas portfolio. Woodside chief executive Liz Westcott outlined the measures during the company’s Capital Markets Day in Sydney on Thursday. The latest savings target represents a $50m increase from the $350m previously announced and will be measured against the company’s 2025 cost base. Woodside expects the workforce reductions to take place over time but has not disclosed which operations or countries will be affected. According to its latest annual workforce figures, the company employed 4,693 people at the end of 2025, including 3,717 in Australia. Besides reducing employee numbers, Woodside intends to simplify internal processes, improve supply chain management and expand the use of artificial intelligence and digital technologies. The restructuring follows portfolio changes involving its Calypso, Sunrise and Bonaparte carbon capture and storage interests. Westcott said the company was concentrating investment on its most profitable assets while improving operating efficiency and capital discipline. The measures come as Woodside prepares to bring several major developments online. Its Scarborough LNG project offshore Western Australia is 99% complete, with the first LNG cargo expected before the end of 2026. The deepwater Trion oil development offshore Mexico is targeting first production in 2028, followed by the Louisiana LNG project in 2029. Woodside expects these developments to support sales growth of more than 30% to approximately 280m barrels of oil equivalent in 2032. The company has also introduced a new shareholder distribution policy targeting payouts of 20% to 40% of adjusted operating cash flow through dividends and potential share buybacks. articles.title: Tech Talk: Wearable Robot for Industrial Workers
articles.summary: A South Korean robotics company is commercializing a lightweight wearable robot designed to reduce physical strain on workers performing repetitive lifting and other demanding tasks, with potential applications in shipbuilding, manufacturing…
articles.body: Tech Talk: Wearable Robot for Industrial Workers Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 Front view of SARTEXO Inc.'s Bionic Suit, built into various types of industrial workwear and a military uniform. Image courtesy KIMM Cheol Hoon Park (far right), CEO of SARTEXO Inc., with researchers from KIMM’s Advanced Robotics Research Center. Image courtesy KIMM Side view of Cheol Hoon Park, CEO of SARTEXO Inc., wearing the Bionic Suit, a clothing-type wearable robot powered by Fabric Muscle. Image courtesy KIMM A South Korean robotics company is commercializing a lightweight wearable robot designed to reduce physical strain on workers performing repetitive lifting and other demanding tasks, with potential applications in shipbuilding, manufacturing, construction and logistics. SARTEXO, a spin-off of the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM), has introduced its Bionic Suit, a third-generation wearable robotic system that uses electrically activated artificial muscles embedded in fabric rather than conventional motors and rigid mechanical frames. The technology, called Fabric Muscle, was developed through research led by SARTEXO CEO Cheol Hoon Park at KIMM beginning in 2012. The system incorporates shape memory alloy (SMA) wires thinner than human hair, formed into spring-like yarn and woven into fabric. When electrical current is applied, the material contracts, generating pulling force that assists the wearer's movements. When the current stops and the material cools, it relaxes. According to KIMM, just 10 grams of Fabric Muscle can lift between 10 and 15 kg, approximately 1,500 times its own weight. The company's Bionic Suit Waist, designed to support the lower back, weighs 1.3 kg including its battery and controller. A full-body version, supporting the lower back, shoulders and elbows simultaneously, weighs no more than 1.8 kg. Testing during repetitive lifting tasks demonstrated reductions in lower-back muscle activity exceeding 40%, according to the developer. Unlike conventional industrial exoskeletons, the fabric-based system can be worn over existing workwear or integrated directly into uniforms. It is also designed for washing and storage. A Fabric Muscle actuator woven from SMA coiled yarn. Image courtesy KIMM

articles.title: StormGeo and CCS launch digital link for maritime emissions verification
articles.summary: StormGeo has partnered with China Classification Society (CCS) to improve the digital exchange and verification of maritime emissions data, strengthening its presence in China’s shipping market. The agreement allows shipping companies using StormGeo’s s-Insight platform to share validated emissions data directly with...
articles.body: StormGeo has partnered with China Classification Society (CCS) to improve the digital exchange and verification of maritime emissions data, strengthening its presence in China’s shipping market. The agreement allows shipping companies using StormGeo’s s-Insight platform to share validated emissions data directly with CCS through an application programming interface (API). As a result, customers can transfer emissions information between the two systems without relying on separate manual data submissions. The connection aims to improve data quality, traceability and efficiency during the verification process. The partnership also supports StormGeo’s wider strategy to expand its maritime technology services in China. Digital integration supports emissions compliance Before the launch, CCS carried out on-site testing to assess the performance and security of StormGeo’s systems. According to the companies, the technology successfully met CCS’s requirements for system integration and interface evaluation. The new connection provides CCS with a structured method for receiving emissions information from StormGeo’s platform. Meanwhile, shipping companies can use the integration to support their environmental compliance procedures. However, the digital exchange of data does not replace the independent verification process carried out by the classification society. Espen Martinsen, Chief Commercial Officer at StormGeo, said the partnership would help the company strengthen its local capabilities and deliver more integrated digital services to Chinese shipping customers. StormGeo currently supports approximately 700 vessels in China with greenhouse gas emissions monitoring and vessel performance services. The company aims to expand its presence in the market as demand for digital environmental compliance solutions continues to develop. Meanwhile, Wei Chong, Manager of Software Development at CCS, highlighted the importance of combining emissions data collection with reliable quality assurance and digital verification systems. The agreement forms part of StormGeo’s broader efforts to improve the exchange of maritime emissions information between shipping companies and verification organisations. By connecting its existing software with CCS’s verification services, StormGeo aims to simplify compliance workflows while supporting the continued digitalisation of China’s maritime sector.

articles.title: Deutsche Windtechnik lands maintenance deal at Germany’s first offshore wind farm
articles.summary: German offshore wind services specialist Deutsche Windtechnik has secured a comprehensive maintenance contract from Ocean Breeze Energy covering all 12 turbines at the Alpha Ventus offshore wind farm in the North Sea. The contract will begin in January 2027 and covers turbine servicing, maintenance, troubleshooting...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables Deutsche Windtechnik lands maintenance deal at Germany’s first offshore wind farm Bojan Lepic November 5, 2026 0 93 1 minute read Alpha Ventus Alpha Ventus German offshore wind services specialist Deutsche Windtechnik has secured a comprehensive maintenance contract from Ocean Breeze Energy covering all 12 turbines at the Alpha Ventus offshore wind farm in the North Sea. The contract will begin in January 2027 and covers turbine servicing, maintenance, troubleshooting and associated technical support. From September 2027, the scope will expand to include remote monitoring, offshore coordination centre services, grid management and around-the-clock alarm handling. The agreement follows Ocean Breeze Energy’s acquisition of Alpha Ventus from EWE, RWE, and Vattenfall in October, with the new owner confirming plans to extend operations at the pioneering German offshore wind development. Commissioned in 2010, Alpha Ventus was Germany’s first offshore wind farm and served as an important testing ground for technologies and maintenance practices subsequently adopted across the country’s offshore wind industry. Located approximately 45 km north of Borkum, the 60 MW development comprises six Senvion 5M turbines and six AREVA Multibrid M5000 units. Deutsche Windtechnik previously provided maintenance services at the project, beginning with the Senvion turbines in 2017 and expanding to the AREVA units in 2020. Both contracts expired at the end of 2024. The new agreement will see the company return to the development under its new ownership structure. Ocean Breeze Energy will retain responsibility for higher-level technical design management. The contract also strengthens Deutsche Windtechnik’s offshore operations around Borkum, where it already provides services at the Riffgat and Trianel Windpark Borkum I projects. articles.title: As Höegh Autoliners Approaches 100, Leif O. Høegh Offers Insights
articles.summary: With plans to celebrate his family’s 100 years in shipping in 2027, Leif O. Høegh, Chair, Höegh Autoliners, takes a moment to reflect on the company’s bold, ‘first mover’ legacy.In 1927, a young Norwegian entrepreneur named Leif Høegh ordered his first vessel, a tanker named Varg.
articles.body: As Höegh Autoliners Approaches 100, Leif O. Høegh Offers Insights Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 Leif O. Høegh, CHAIR, Höegh Autoliners Photo credit: Javad Moghimi Pars With plans to celebrate his family’s 100 years in shipping in 2027, Leif O. Høegh, Chair, Höegh Autoliners, takes a moment to reflect on the company’s bold, ‘first mover’ legacy. In 1927, a young Norwegian entrepreneur named Leif Høegh ordered his first vessel, a tanker named Varg. Backed by the legendary Danish shipowner A.P Møller, the fledgling company survived the Great Depression (and later, World War II) to operate a small fleet of oil tankers. But by the 1960s, the company began to diversify, entering new shipping segments. “Not all these investments paid off,” said Leif O. Høegh, Chair. “Over the years, we have been involved in everything from cargo ships to LPG carriers, passenger ships to fishing trawlers, and many other projects now lost in the mist of time. In fact, the company has only accumulated capital in maybe the last 20 years of our history.” Learning from experience While Høegh acknowledges the company’s history sometimes saddled the company with excess debt, he insists that the company’s willingness to take risks in people, technology and commercial solutions has been the key to its success. “If you don’t take any risks, you don’t learn anything,” he says. “And in today’s environment, as much as in any of the last 100 years, being willing to go first can be an advantage.” Høegh explains that the company’s entry into the car carrier market grew out of its operation of lift-on/lift-off cargo ships in the 1960s. In 1970, the company formed a joint venture with Ugland to create Höegh-Ugland Auto Liners (HUAL). “HUAL would go on to pioneer the development of roll on roll off vessels and later, Pure Car Truck Carriers (PCTC) in the 1980s,” he says. “In 2000, we acquired Ugland’s stake in the company and five years later, rebranded the company Höegh Autoliners. Since then, we have continued to push the boundaries of this vessel class.” Sustainability as Strategy In addition to advanced vessel design to improve flexibility and increase capacity, Höegh Autoliners has placed sustainability at the core of its business strategy. For example, the company’s six high-capacity Horizon class vessels, delivered in 2015 and 2016, were engineered to emit about 50 per cent less CO2 per unit transported compared to standard, conventional car carriers. “As an inherent business value, sustainability lies at the core of Höegh Autoliners’ operations,” he says. “For us, it is not just about compliance, but sustainability leadership.” But perhaps the company’s biggest innovation to date has been placing an order for 18 multi-fuel Aurora class PCTCs, with an option to add four more. “As the first in the PCTC segment to receive DNV’s ammonia-ready and methanol-ready notations, the Auroras are capable of operating with zero emissions,” he says. “They are the crown jewels of our ground-breaking fleet renewal programme.” Høegh is aware that optionality costs money but notes that the vessels the company builds today will be operating for up to 30 years. “Shipping is a capital-intensive industry, so when we consider what the next decades, or ideally the next 100 years, will look like for us, it’s all about what decisions we will be able to make in five, 10 or 20 years from now,” he says. “You have to get comfortable with the idea that your option premium might be worthless, but that does not mean the decision was a bad one or that the option has no value.” Embracing Uncertainty Høegh says there is a tendency for some people to get overly nervous about all the various unpredictable and hard-to-understand trends in the world. “We have seen a lot of changes in the last century and today is no different,” he says. “We can’t know or control what fuels will be available, how shifting geopolitics will impact the industry or what we can expect as AI develops. You can either think of these things as a series of threats or a series of opportunities, but waiting to find out isn’t a strategy. You must put capital to work and focus on what you can control, from big decisions on vessel design to providing safe, meaningful work for employees and seafarers alike.” In a highly conservative industry, first movers are often punished, but Høegh believes not everyone can be a smart follower. “The risk matrix analysis they teach in business school will tell you it’s always better to be a smart follower,” he says. “But we have been rewarded for taking risks in the past and I am confident that being a first mover will not only make us more resilient in a changing world it will also show the industry that it can be done. So, in addition to building the Auroras, we are working in partnership with world-leading ammonia and methanol distributors to ensure reliable supply, and with our customers to decarbonise their supply chains.” Nor-Shipping 2027 Like other players in the industry, Höegh Autoliners relies on a network of suppliers to push the technology forward. And as a main partner of Nor-Shipping 2027, Høegh recognizes that the exhibition provides an important arena for bringing people, ideas, and perspective from across ocean industries together in one place. “For us, Nor-Shipping 2027 will be a valuable opportunity to connect with partners, contribute to the conversation, and showcase the solutions needed for a more sustainable maritime future,” he says. “And despite increasing geopolitical uncertainty, we cannot give up on the institutions, shared principles and networked, global perspectives that make our industry unique.”

articles.body: Asia Europe Middle East Offshore Aker Solutions bags engineering deal for Qatar oilfield redevelopment Bojan Lepic November 5, 2026 0 238 1 minute read Aker Solutions Aker Solutions Norwegian offshore engineering group Aker Solutions has received a letter of award from Vietnam’s PTSC Mechanical & Construction for work on QatarEnergy’s Maydan Mahzam oilfield redevelopment project. The contract covers detailed engineering for three major topsides, four jackets and modifications required to connect new facilities with existing offshore infrastructure. Aker Solutions describes the award as sizeable, valuing it between NOK500m and NOK1.5bn ($54m to $162m). The company will carry out engineering work from its offices in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Mumbai, India. The award remains subject to a final contract, with Aker Solutions expecting to register the order in its Renewables and Field Development segment during the fourth quarter of 2026. The Maydan Mahzam field lies around 100 km northeast of Qatar’s coastline, in water depths of approximately 40 metres. Discovered in the 1960s, the field began producing in 1965. QatarEnergy is undertaking a major redevelopment to modernise ageing offshore facilities, improve production efficiency and extend the field’s operating life. PTSC M&C secured the project’s first major offshore construction package in September and signed the main contract with QatarEnergy on October 22. The Vietnamese contractor’s responsibilities include engineering, procurement, fabrication, transportation, installation and commissioning of eight offshore structures weighing more than 100,000 tonnes combined. The programme is scheduled to run from the fourth quarter of 2026 until the end of 2031 and is designed to help sustain Maydan Mahzam production at approximately 25,000 barrels per day. articles.body: Europe Middle East Offshore Renewables HEA Energy snaps up Subsea7’s six-ship heavy transport business Adis Ajdin November 5, 2026 0 504 1 minute read Seaway7 Seaway7 Abu Dhabi-based HEA Energy has struck a deal to acquire Subsea7’s heavy transportation business, adding a six-vessel operation to its growing offshore fleet. The transaction will see Subsea7’s offshore renewables arm Seaway7 divest a business comprising five owned and one chartered open-deck semi-submersible heavy transport vessels. The fleet includes Seaway Eagle, Seaway Falcon, Seaway Hawk, Seaway Osprey, Seaway Albatross and the chartered Seaway Swan . The vessels are used to transport offshore wind foundations, substations, jackup rigs, offshore modules and other oversized cargo, with lifting and transportation capabilities covering loads of up to 55,000 tonnes. Financial terms have not been disclosed, with Subsea7 saying the transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals. Completion is expected in the first half of 2027. The sale forms part of the permitted divestments under Subsea7’s merger agreement with Italian offshore contractor Saipem and will trigger a €105m special dividend to Subsea7 shareholders. For HEA Energy, the acquisition marks another major expansion of its offshore vessel business, which has been growing rapidly across the Middle East and Europe. The company was established in 2022 by Hassan Elali, the founder and former executive chairman of Zakher Marine International (ZMI), which was acquired by ADNOC Logistics & Services. HEA has been building up its offshore support and wind maintenance fleet through newbuildings and acquisitions. By September this year, the company had 19 vessels delivered and another 12 under construction, with deliveries scheduled through 2027. Its expansion has also included offshore wind maintenance work in Europe, where the company has secured contracts involving its jackup vessels, including HEA Hercules , which was mobilised for a North Sea campaign earlier this year. The divestment comes as Subsea7 and Saipem work towards their proposed merger to create Saipem7. articles.title: Finland jails captain and crew member over Baltic cable sabotage
articles.summary: A Finnish court has sentenced the captain and a crew member of the general cargo ship Fitburg to prison for deliberately damaging two subsea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland on New Year’s Eve last year. Helsinki District Court handed Russian captain Andrei Maksimenko a three-and-a-half-year prison...
articles.body: Europe Operations Regulatory Finland jails captain and crew member over Baltic cable sabotage Adis Ajdin November 5, 2026 0 580 2 minutes read Finnish Border Guard Finnish Border Guard A Finnish court has sentenced the captain and a crew member of the general cargo ship Fitburg to prison for deliberately damaging two subsea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland on New Year’s Eve last year. Helsinki District Court handed Russian captain Andrei Maksimenko a three-and-a-half-year prison sentence, while Azerbaijani bosun Vusal Majidov received two years and 10 months after both were convicted of aggravated criminal damage. The court ordered the two men, who had been subject to travel bans during proceedings, to be taken into custody immediately. They were also ordered to pay compensation for the damage caused to subsea infrastructure. The case centres on the St Vincent and the Grenadines-flagged Fitburg , which was intercepted by Finnish authorities on December 31, 2025, while sailing from St Petersburg to Israel carrying steel products. Investigators established that the vessel had dragged its damaged anchor and chain along the seabed for around 130 km, damaging two telecommunications cables belonging to Elisa and Arelion Finland. The anchor also crossed seven other telecommunications and power cables and a gas pipeline, creating a risk of further damage to critical infrastructure. The court found that the anchor had been lowered after the ship departed St Petersburg but before it left Russian territorial waters. Although prosecutors did not claim that the captain had personally ordered the anchor lowered, the court ruled that both men must have known it was dragging while the vessel continued its voyage. It also found that the bosun had actively contributed to the ship continuing for around two hours after Finnish authorities first contacted the vessel. Both defendants denied wrongdoing and challenged Finland’s jurisdiction, arguing that the damage occurred outside its territorial waters. The court rejected that argument, ruling that Finnish courts could hear the case because the offences were intentional and their consequences were felt in Finland. The decision comes after a separate case involving the Cook Islands-flagged tanker Eagle S , whose crew faced charges over damage to five undersea cables in December 2024. Helsinki District Court initially dismissed that case on jurisdictional grounds in October 2025, but an appeals court overturned the decision in August this year and ordered the case to be reconsidered. The Fitburg defendants were also charged with aggravated interference with telecommunications, but the court dismissed that separate count because it was covered by the aggravated criminal damage conviction. The ruling is not final. The captain’s lawyer has indicated that he intends to appeal, while the bosun is also considering challenging the verdict. The Qingdao-based owner’s Singapore subsidiary has agreed to acquire the 4,981 gt Jia Yue Ming Zhu , which was built in October this year and will be renamed Golden Canna. The vessel is being purchased from Marshall Islands-incorporated Sanhe Jiaye, according to a filing with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. Seacon will pay a $2.94m deposit upon delivery, with the remaining $16.66m due within 120 days. The acquisition will be funded through internal resources and external financing. The latest purchase follows shipbroking reports linking Seacon to the sale of four MR product tankers in an en bloc deal involving two recently completed vessels and another two still under construction. The company has not publicly confirmed the reported transaction. Seacon has been actively reshaping its tanker portfolio, combining investments in newer chemical and product carriers with vessel sales and refinancing deals. In June, the company agreed to acquire two chemical and oil tankers, Golden Gerbera and Golden Osmanthus , from Oriental Prime Shipping for $39.2m, or $19.6m apiece. The owner also carried out a $103.4m refinancing of four 18,500 dwt chemical tankers in August, replacing earlier sale-and-leaseback arrangements with new 10-year facilities at lower financing margins. Seacon’s push into larger product tankers dates back to 2024, when it contracted four 50,000 dwt MR vessels at Chengxi Shipyard for around $45m each. The group was subsequently linked to another four MR newbuildings through a joint venture with Huanghai Shipbuilding. At the end of June, Seacon controlled 38 vessels and held investments in another 15 through joint ventures, with its diversified portfolio including 18 oil and chemical tankers. articles.title: Iran’s Empty Tankers Sit Idle as Visible Crude Loadings Stop
articles.summary: Six Weeks Without a Visible Loading No Iran-affiliated tanker still transmitting AIS in the Middle East Gulf has shown a draft change indicative of loading since September 17. Before then, MIOC detected only seven AIS-transmitting tankers loading almost 6 million barrels between July 27 and September 17, a pace of...
articles.body: Iran’s Empty Tankers Sit Idle as Visible Crude Loadings Stop in International Shipping News 05/11/2026 Six Weeks Without a Visible Loading No Iran-affiliated tanker still transmitting AIS in the Middle East Gulf has shown a draft change indicative of loading since September 17. Before then, MIOC detected only seven AIS-transmitting tankers loading almost 6 million barrels between July 27 and September 17, a pace of around 113,000 barrels per day. Satellite imagery points the same way. Automated detection over Kharg Island from September 18 to November 1 found no dark tanker at either of the island’s loading terminals. Dark vessels are holding the same nine positions in the anchorage east of Kharg Island, where tankers wait to load at Kharg. Spare Capacity Sits Unused Inside the Gulf Windward data shows 47 tankers in the Middle East Gulf that are owned by the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) or the National Iranian Tanker Company (NITC), fly Iran’s flag, or have made Iranian port calls in 2026. Only 25 of them still broadcast AIS, and 22 are dark, 14 of them since the blockade began. The figures that follow describe only the 25 tankers still transmitting, not Iran’s entire commercial tanker fleet. Of those 25, 15 (60%) appear to be in ballast, and 11 of them are VLCCs. Together they have nearly 24 million barrels of empty capacity. Another nine, including three VLCCs, sit laden with about 11 million barrels aboard. The load state of one is undetermined. Iran’s AIS-transmitting tankers in the Gulf have room to spare, but none of them has loaded since September 17. Three Explanations for Where the Crude Is Going There is no evidence showing where Iran’s crude is going instead, which leaves three possible explanations. The first is that crude is moving into onshore tanks at Kharg Island. The second is that tankers are loading while dark, between satellite passes. Either would only postpone the problem of Iran having limited capacity to keep its crude. The third is that Iran has cut output and begun capping wells. This would be its worst case, since it would risk equipment damage, add repair time, and raise the cost of bringing the wells back online. Iran’s Old Floating Storage Now Sits Empty Outside the Middle East Gulf, the AIS-visible tankers that once served as Iran’s floating storage prior to delivering their cargo now sit largely empty. Windward data shows 140 Iran-linked tankers broadcasting AIS outside the Gulf, of which 115 are in ballast, and 25 are laden. Five main holding areas account for 76 of those tankers, off Malaysia’s Eastern Outer Port Limits, Sri Lanka, eastern Malaysia, Karachi, and Duqm. Only three of the 76 are laden or partly laden, according to available AIS draft data. Laden AIS-transmitting Iran-associated tankers across Asia and the Indian Ocean carry about 9.6 million barrels. About 5.9 million barrels of that, or 61%, is in transit aboard five tankers heading toward China. What to Watch Each of the three explanations leaves a trace. A tanker anchored east of Kharg that changes position or draft between satellite passes would point to dark loading. Continued silence at the terminals would put more weight on onshore storage and, as those tanks fill, on output cuts. The longer the gap runs past six weeks, the narrower Iran’s options become. articles.title: BIMCO: Tripartite 2026 focuses on practical steps towards the next generation of ships
articles.summary: Regulatory clarity, decarbonisation and digitalisation were central to discussions as more than 85 representatives of shipbuilders, shipowners and classification societies, together with invited observers, met in Tokyo on 28–29 October for Tripartite 2026. BIMCO was this year’s organising association. The annual...
articles.body: BIMCO: Tripartite 2026 focuses on practical steps towards the next generation of ships in International Shipping News 05/11/2026 Regulatory clarity, decarbonisation and digitalisation were central to discussions as more than 85 representatives of shipbuilders, shipowners and classification societies, together with invited observers, met in Tokyo on 28–29 October for Tripartite 2026. BIMCO was this year’s organising association. The annual summit examined how the industry can develop safe, secure and environmentally sustainable ships amid technological change and regulatory uncertainty. Participants reaffirmed their support for the International Maritime Organization (IMO) as shipping’s global regulator and stressed that close cooperation between regulators, shipbuilders, shipowners and classification societies is essential to making new requirements clear and workable. “Tripartite brings together shipbuilders, shipowners and classification societies to discuss contemporary issues related to new ships. By sharing hands-on experience and working together through this unique forum, we contribute with realistic solutions that can be implemented effectively across the industry to deliver on the ambitions of the regulators at IMO,” Lars Robert Pedersen, BIMCO Deputy Secretary General Clearer rules for new technologies and fuels Discussions covered fuel efficiency, new technologies and practical approaches to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Participants considered how safety regulation can keep pace with new fuels and novel propulsion systems, alongside the need for greater harmonisation across regulatory requirements and progress towards a single global decarbonisation framework. A high-level panel explored how the industry can build the next generation of ships despite uncertainty over future regulation. A dedicated session also examined nuclear technology and its potential role in maritime decarbonisation. Better data exchange and less administration Digitalisation discussions focused on reducing administrative burdens, improving information exchange between ship and shore, and using data more effectively to support safe and efficient operations. Participants also discussed data interoperability between ships, shore-based teams and other stakeholders, and a common environmental reporting protocol covering local, regional and commercial requirements. Environmental sessions addressed current compliance challenges and emerging regulatory requirements. Turning discussions into practical outcomes Tripartite’s working groups will continue to develop solutions and recommendations on technical, safety, environmental and digitalisation issues. Their work supports the safe, sustainable and efficient operation of ships and related regulatory developments at IMO. The forum has supported IMO’s work for more than two decades, contributing to Common Structural Rules for bulk carriers and tankers, permanent means of access on tankers, and mandatory coatings for ballast and cargo tanks. The participating organisations are ASEF, BIMCO, CESA, IACS, ICS, INTERCARGO, INTERTANKO and SEA Europe. This year’s summit was also sponsored and supported by ClassNK, the Japanese Shipowners’ Association and the Shipbuilders’ Association of Japan. The next Tripartite forum will take place in China in the fourth quarter of 2027. articles.title: What Trump’s midterm elections defeat could mean for the IMO shipping climate negotiations
articles.summary: The Democratic victory in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov 3, taking control of both the House and the Senate, could have important indirect implications for the US stance and behaviour at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). Experts say the results are part of a broader shift back toward climate...
articles.body: What Trump’s midterm elections defeat could mean for the IMO shipping climate negotiations in International Shipping News 05/11/2026 The Democratic victory in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov 3, taking control of both the House and the Senate, could have important indirect implications for the US stance and behaviour at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). Experts say the results are part of a broader shift back toward climate action, following Lula’s re-election in Brazil in October. It’s a signal of constructive future US re-engagement in global climate diplomacy, including cutting emissions from ships at the IMO. The Democrats will also be able to wield Congressional oversight over the Trump administration, forcing greater transparency and accountability. This could make it more difficult for Trump’s representatives to mix commercial and political interests and to threaten economic retaliation against other countries, according to experts. The Democrats won the elections by campaigning around issues like lowering living costs, expanding clean energy and acting as a legislative check on executive power. Why this matters: The Trump administration has been one of the leading opponents to the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a key climate policy designed to cut emissions from ships. In October 2025, US delegates derailed the NZF’s planned adoption by deploying “shocking” and “undiplomatic” tactics and illegal threats on countries and individual delegates, but failed to scrap the agreement entirely. The IMO is set to debate the adoption of the NZF again, at a two-part summit starting this month: technical negotiations (ISWG-GHG-23) on 23-27 November and political negotiations (MEPC 85) on 30 November – 4 December. Jamie Yates, Climate & Renewable Energy Manager, Pacific Environment, said: “U.S. voters are rejecting backward energy policies that drove up household costs and undoubtedly accelerated the effects of climate disasters. At every turn, the Trump administration has tried to put the brakes on global shipping decarbonization. We urge IMO Member States to reject delay tactics and formally adopt the Net-Zero Framework. The world has already lost a year in climate action from shipping; it cannot afford another.” Aoife O’Leary, CEO of Opportunity Green, says: “The tectonic plates of power at the IMO are shifting. The United States, the biggest opponent to the IMO Net Zero Framework last year, has just held an election that signals a far greater interest in climate action than we might have thought. At the same time, Brazil, a key architect of the framework, secured another four-year mandate to push for global climate action. We are in a different context than October 2025, and countries must capitalise on this momentum at the IMO to finally get the Net Zero Framework over the finishing line and steer shipping towards a just and equitable transition away from fossil fuels.” Christiaan De Beukelaer, University of Melbourne, said: “The Trump Administration lost a mandate to continue its obstructive stance at the IMO. This creates space for others to step up and get the Net-Zero Framework adopted later this month. All eyes on China, Brazil and the EU. The time for further preemptive compromises to appease Washington is gone, now countries can and must deliver decisive action to implement the IMO climate strategy they committed to.” Source: Pacific Environment, Opportunity Green, University of Melbourne 2026-11-05 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Maersk converts market opportunities into significantly higher earnings and raises full-year guidance in International Shipping News 05/11/2026 Against a backdrop of resilient trade flows and congestion-driven capacity constraints, Maersk’s strong commercial and operational execution drove revenue growth and significantly higher earnings, while helping customers navigate continued supply chain disruption. Executive Summary Full-year guidance raised to an underlying EBITDA of USD 14.0-14.5bn (previously USD 10.5-12.5bn) and an underlying EBIT of USD 8.0-8.5bn (previously USD 4.5-6.5bn) For the group, EBITDA was USD 4.7bn and EBIT was USD 3.3bn in the third quarter, up on both the prior year and second quarter Ocean generated significantly better earnings, driven by steady volumes and higher freight rates Logistics & Services grew revenue by 13% and improved EBIT margin to 5.8% Terminals achieved record-high revenue and maintained strong earnings Continued execution of the USD 1.0bn share buy-back programme CEO Statement Vincent Clerc, Chief Executive Officer at Maersk: “We delivered a strong quarter across our businesses. Despite continued geopolitical uncertainty and disruptions, global trade has remained remarkably resilient. Demand is being driven not only by consumer spending, but increasingly by major investments in electrification, energy and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, generating significant flows of industrial cargo around the world. We have been well positioned to capture this demand, with our vessel fleet operating at full capacity and demand exceeding available space on certain routes. This reflects both the underlying strength of global trade and the tremendous job our colleagues are doing every day to deliver for our customers.” Q3 highlights The global economy maintained resilient and broad-based growth in Q3, and global container demand grew between 2% and 4% year-on-year. Asian exports saw a deceleration in July and August amidst weather-related disruptions. On the import side, softer demand growth in Europe and the drag exerted by Middle Eastern imports were partially offset by solid growth in Africa, Latin America and North America. The quarter was marked by a severe typhoon season in Asia resulting in substantial port congestion that absorbed a sizeable amount of vessel capacity. At its peak, global average port waiting times reached 16.6 hours, the highest level since January 2023. As a result, average spot freight rates, as measured by the Shanghai Containerised Freight Index were up 46% in Q3 relative to the previous quarter. Strong commercial and operational execution enabled Maersk to translate the market conditions into a 27% year-on-year increase in revenue to USD 18.1bn, driven by all three businesses. Group EBITDA rose from USD 2.7bn to USD 4.7bn, while EBIT increased from USD 1.3bn to USD 3.3bn, bringing the EBIT margin to 18.1%. Ocean continued to leverage the favourable market pushing EBIT up to USD 2.6bn (USD 567m). Despite adverse weather conditions in Asia constraining capacity and loadings, loaded volumes remained high, with vessel utilisation remaining at 96%. The continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz and widespread network congestion increased bunker, network and container handling costs and affected schedule reliability. Logistics & Services revenue grew by 13%, supported by strong volume development across most products, elevated rates, and landbridge solutions in the Middle-East. Landside was the largest contributor to growth, driven by landbridge solutions across the Gulf region. Forwarding also performed strongly, with solid volume growth in Air and Project Logistics, while Contract Logistics continued to deliver revenue growth within Solutions. Profitability improved year-on-year, with the EBIT margin increasing to 5.8% from 5.5% reflecting disciplined cost management and solid operational execution. Terminals confirmed its strong position, delivering record-high revenue. Volumes increased by 2.6%, supported by growth in Africa and Europe of 14% and 6.7% respectively. Utilisation was 85% (90%). Adjusted for a concession extension-related impairment reversal recognised in 2025, the EBIT margin increased by 0.5 percentage points from 32.0% to 32.5%. Investments In late August, APM Terminals broke ground on the new Laldia greenfield terminal in Chattogram, Bangladesh. The landmark project will add 900,000 TEU of annual port capacity. In September, APM Terminals Suape commenced operations in Pernambuco, Brazil, with the arrival of the first commercial vessel. The new greenfield terminal increases the capacity of the Suape Port Complex by 55%, initially adding up to 400,000 TEU of annual handling capacity. As part of its fleet renewal programme, Maersk ordered 26 dual-fuel container vessels, each with a capacity of 18,600 TEU. The vessels are scheduled for delivery in 2029 and 2030. Financial guidance Maersk has updated its full-year 2026 financial guidance on the back of the actual performance in the third quarter of 2026 and improved visibility for the remainder of the year. This is based on global container market volume growth for the full year 2026 of around 4% Source: Maersk 2026-11-05 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: IEA, IEF, and OPEC convene industry experts for crucial dialogue on maritime energy flows
articles.summary: The International Energy Agency (IEA), the International Energy Forum (IEF), and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) today convened key stakeholders and leading industry experts to discuss maritime energy flows, shipping and insurance in a ‘Joint IEA-IEF-OPEC Technical Workshop on the...
articles.body: IEA, IEF, and OPEC convene industry experts for crucial dialogue on maritime energy flows in International Shipping News 05/11/2026 The International Energy Agency (IEA), the International Energy Forum (IEF), and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) today convened key stakeholders and leading industry experts to discuss maritime energy flows, shipping and insurance in a ‘Joint IEA-IEF-OPEC Technical Workshop on the Security of Energy Flows: Maritime Routes and Market Stability’. The technical workshop comes at the request of the consultation meeting of ministers of the Declaration of Cooperation (DoC) which was held in Riyadh on 12 October 2026, following the IEF17. At that meeting, ministers underlined the critical importance of ensuring uninterrupted flows of energy, expressed concern about elevated shipping and insurance costs, and noted their wish to continue engaging with the IEF, the IEA and other international partners on these issues. The technical workshop builds on the IEA-IEF-OPEC trilateral programme of work and their shared concerns such as reflected in the IEF 17 Ministerial Concluding Statement, including the protection of energy infrastructure and trade routes. Today’s online meeting was convened under the leadership of OPEC Secretary General, HE Haitham Al Ghais, IEA Executive Director, HE Dr. Fatih Birol and IEF Secretary General, HE Eng. Jassim Alshirawi. In highlighting the importance of the meeting, HE Al Ghais said: “Participants in the DoC remain fully committed to supporting the stability of global energy markets. In this regard, our discussions will be vital to help identify possible solutions to the challenges facing both producers and consumers in relation to current maritime trade.” HE Al Ghais also stressed that maritime energy flows remain a core pillar of global energy security and noted that shipping and insurance costs in 2026 have increased significantly to a level of more than one-third of the underlying value of crude oil. Furthermore, the elevated transportation and risk expenses have been passed along the entire oil and energy value chains, straining both producing and consuming economies, and placing additional inflationary pressures on the global economy. HE Birol said “Energy markets are facing a crisis of unprecedented proportions, affecting the production and transportation of the oil and gas on which the global economy relies. While producers have worked hard to maintain supply, under extremely difficult circumstances, we must all work to safeguard freedom of maritime navigation, a central pillar of global energy security. That is why we are here today, together with our colleagues from OPEC and the IEF, to help find durable solutions to these challenges.” HE Alshirawi said “Safe maritime passage is essential to energy security and market stability for producers, consumers and transit countries alike. Disruption can raise energy, food and transport costs far beyond the region affected, with the greatest hardship falling on vulnerable communities. Building on IEF17, our cooperation with the IEA and OPEC can strengthen the dialogue and data transparency needed to restore confidence, support investment and build more resilient global energy markets.” Today’s workshop underscores the flexibility of the joint programme of work agreed upon by the IEA, the IEF and OPEC and endorsed by energy ministers at the 12th International Energy Forum, held in Cancún, Mexico in March 2010, as part of the ‘Cancún Declaration’. articles.body: New LR service targets cargo disruption when trade routes fail in International Shipping News 05/11/2026 New LR Advisory service helps ports, governments and logistics operators respond to disruption, protect critical cargo flows and strengthen trade corridor resilience Lloyd’s Register (LR) Advisory has launched a new Supply Chain Resilience service to help ports, governments and logistics operators keep critical cargo moving when geopolitical shocks, congestion, extreme weather or infrastructure failures disrupt established trade routes. When a critical port, border or transport link becomes constrained, disruption can quickly spread across the wider logistics network. Alternative gateways may lack capacity, diversions can add cost and delay, and pressure can shift from ports to road, rail and other inland connections. Launched today at the IAPH2026 World Ports Conference in London, LR’s new service addresses these dependencies across the complete supply chain, helping clients determine where cargo should move, which alternatives are viable and when contingency measures should be activated. Kamran Ul Haq, Senior Vice President, LR Ports Advisory LR Advisory assesses disruption across ports, airports, road borders and rail connections, identifying where pressure on one part of the network could create new bottlenecks elsewhere. It then helps clients compare alternative gateways and sea, air and land transport combinations against cost, capacity, delay, service and risk. In the first 0–90 days of a disruption, LR can carry out a rapid assessment of affected routes and develop a 30–60–90 day response plan. This can include alternative routing, cargo prioritisation, diversion triggers, surge-capacity measures and clear operating rules that allow clients to adapt as conditions change. For essential and time-sensitive shipments, including food, medicines, energy supplies, industrial inputs and exports, LR Advisory can help determine which cargo should move first and how available capacity should be used. Alternative sea, sea-air, sea-land and air-land routes can be assessed, including bonded and cross-border options where feasible. Kamran Ul Haq, Senior Vice President, LR Ports Advisory, said: “The worst time to discover that an alternative route cannot handle the cargo you need to move is after your main gateway has already been disrupted. “Diverting cargo is rarely as simple as choosing another port. Capacity, inland connections, border processes, cost and availability all matter. Our role is to give clients a clear view of those trade-offs, identify workable alternatives and establish the triggers for action before disruption spreads further through the network.” The service also helps clients translate lessons from short-term disruption into longer-term decisions about their logistics networks and infrastructure. Over a three-month to five-year horizon, LR Advisory can assess how corridor diversification and infrastructure development could reduce reliance on individual gateways and chokepoints. This includes resilience planning for port, airport, road and rail interfaces, together with feasibility and investment planning for infrastructure such as dry ports, inland logistics hubs and rail-connected freight nodes. Kamran added: “Resilience is not about trying to predict where the next disruption will come from. It is about understanding where a supply chain is vulnerable and having credible alternatives ready before they are needed. “That means looking beyond the immediate diversion. The decisions made during a disruption can reveal where future investment, additional capacity or greater corridor diversity could make the whole network more resilient.” Source: Lloyd’s Register 2026-11-05 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: When a critical port, border or transport link becomes constrained, disruption can quickly spread across the wider logistics network.
Alternative gateways may lack capacity, diversions can add cost and delay, and pressure can shift from ports to road, rail and other inland connections.
It then helps clients compare alternative gateways and sea, air and land transport combinations against cost, capacity, delay, service and risk.

articles.body: Steamship Mutual returns US$39m to Members, taking total returns to US$198m over the past 10 years in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 05/11/2026 Steamship Mutual has reaffirmed its commitment to its Members with the Board approving a distribution of 10%, equivalent to US$39m, as part of its February 2027 renewal. At the eight-month point, the Club’s claims for the 2026/27 policy year show significant improvement on the corresponding position last year. At six months, four claims were reported to the IG Pool that exceed Club retention. The Club’s claims for prior years have been better than expected across all areas of its business alongside favourable prior IG Pool claims development. Responsible capital management delivering Member value Steamship’s approach to capital distribution reflects its commitment to prudent stewardship and the long-term interests of the Membership. The Club’s investment strategy prioritises capital preservation while retaining flexibility to respond to market conditions. Approximately 60% of the investment portfolio is held in government and corporate bonds, with this approach delivering significant income. A long-term approach centred on Members Commenting on the Club’s strategy, Buckley McAlister, Chair of Steamship Mutual, said “Our responsibility is to manage the Club for the long-term benefit of its Members. At the February 2026 renewal, following an exceptional period of claims activity, retaining capital was the right decision to protect the strength of the Club. The measures taken at that renewal are contributing to the improved current-year claims performance we are seeing today. The Club’s capital position has strengthened again this year, allowing the Board to continue its policy of returning excess capital to its Members while prudently maintaining capital adequacy, in line with our commitment to mutuality. This means the Club has returned $198m over the past decade.” Rupert Harris, Chief Underwriting Officer, said “The decision to make a capital distribution alongside an inflationary 4% general increase, reflects two important responsibilities of the mutual model. The 4% general increase for the 2027 policy year supports our objective of achieving a stable underwriting performance, while maintaining fairness across the Membership. articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables Vattenfall signs final agreements for 1.8GW Danish offshore wind projects Bojan Lepic November 5, 2026 0 140 1 minute read Vattenfall Vattenfall Swedish energy group Vattenfall has signed final agreements with the Danish Energy Agency for two offshore wind developments with a combined capacity of at least 1.8GW. The agreements cover the 800 MW Hesselø project in the Kattegat and the 1 GW Holmsland development in the North Sea, both expected to become operational in 2032. Holmsland was previously known as North Sea I Mid, with the name changed to reflect its location off the Danish coast near Hvide Sande. The signing follows Vattenfall’s successful bids for both projects in Denmark’s offshore wind tender in August. The company secured the North Sea project with a bid of DKK504 ($78) per MWh, while its winning offer for Hesselø was DKK542 ($84) per MWh. The agreed prices are guaranteed for 20 years after the developments are completed. Hesselø is located approximately 30 km from the Danish coast, while Holmsland is planned around 20 km offshore. Together, the projects are expected to significantly expand the country’s offshore renewable energy capacity. The company stressed that construction of both wind farms remains subject to final investment decisions and the necessary regulatory approvals. Vattenfall currently operates five offshore wind farms in Denmark, generating about 6.5TWh of electricity annually. The company is also developing major offshore wind projects elsewhere in Europe, including Nordlicht in Germany and Zeevonk in the Netherlands. BP chief executive Meg O’Neill said the Norwegian producer’s performance and favourable market conditions created an opportunity to realise some of the investment’s value. Aker BP was established in 2016 by combining BP’s Norwegian upstream business with Det norske oljeselskap. The company has since become one of Norway’s largest independent oil and gas producers, with a portfolio of producing assets and developments across the Norwegian continental shelf. Aker BP reported production of 374,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in the third quarter, while its major Yggdrasil and Valhall PWP-Fenris developments remain on track for first production in mid-2027. articles.body: Pacific International Lines (PIL) has ordered seven new methanol-ready feeder containerships from Huanghai Shipbuilding in China, as part of its fleet renewal and expansion programme. Each vessel will have a capacity of 1,400 TEU, bringing the combined capacity of the order to 9,800 TEU. Deliveries are scheduled between 2029 and 2030. The new ships will strengthen PIL’s regional shipping network, particularly its Intra-Asia and Pacific Islands services. They will also support connections between smaller ports and major transshipment hubs. According to the Singapore-based carrier, the vessels have been designed to meet the specific operational requirements of these regional markets. Illustration of PIL’s 1,400 TEU vessel_MR New feeder vessels designed for regional operations The seven containerships will measure 172 metres in length and 25 metres in width. Their dimensions have been customised to maximise capacity while maintaining flexibility when serving smaller ports. In addition, the vessels will feature energy-saving technologies to improve propulsion efficiency and reduce fuel consumption. These include pre-swirl vanes and propeller boss cap fins, which are designed to improve water flow around the propeller. The ships will also feature enhanced cargo safety equipment, including fixed fire water monitors and cargo hold water spray systems. Furthermore, the vessels will incorporate digital technologies to support operational monitoring and vessel performance. Lars Kastrup, Chief Executive Officer of PIL, said the investment would strengthen the carrier’s capacity across its Intra-Asia and Pacific Islands network. He also highlighted the importance of improving operational efficiency while supporting PIL’s long-term environmental objectives. PIL continues fleet renewal programme The new containerships will be methanol-ready, allowing PIL to prepare for the potential future adoption of lower-emission fuels. However, the announcement does not confirm that the ships will be equipped with methanol dual-fuel engines upon delivery. The order forms part of PIL’s wider fleet renewal strategy, which aims to improve efficiency and support its target of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050. Huanghai Shipbuilding was selected for its technical capabilities and experience, according to PIL. The carrier has not disclosed the financial value of the contract. Once delivered, the seven vessels will provide additional feeder capacity for PIL’s regional operations and support cargo connections across its international network.

articles.title: Energy security to keep running the show into 2027 amid market shifts, IEA Chief warns
articles.summary: $3.4 trillion global energy spend: Clean tech outpaces fossil fuels nearly 2-to-1 in 2026. IEA Chief says energy markets will not normalize in 2027.
articles.body: Market Outlooks November 5, 2026 · 2 hours ago Energy security to keep running the show into 2027 amid market shifts, IEA Chief warns $3.4 trillion global energy spend: Clean tech outpaces fossil fuels nearly 2-to-1 in 2026. IEA Chief says energy markets will not normalize in 2027. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 5 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: IEA As the energy transition reshapes capital allocation, global energy spending is barreling toward a record $3.4 trillion, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). However, IEA’s Executive Director has warned that markets will not return to normal in 2027, as energy security continues to shake up global markets. With the Middle East conflict exposing severe supply vulnerabilities as shipping transit through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a halt, the crisis has highlighted the critical need to diversify supplies and find new delivery routes. While low-emissions technologies, nuclear, storage, and grid expansions pull in $2.2 trillion, leaving traditional oil, gas, and coal trailing behind, fossil fuel extraction is continuing to command a $1.2 trillion slice of the market. Driven by persistent geopolitical energy shocks, global investments are fuelling a nuclear comeback and a surge in clean infrastructure deployment looking toward 2027. As reported by Reuters , Fatih Birol , IEA’s Executive Director, recently warned that markets would not revert to pre-war conditions in 2027. Highlighting persistent supply security risks, high fuel pressures, and a rush toward clean tech and nuclear resilience, the ongoing supply vulnerabilities and diesel and gas constraints across Europe appear to be bringing in a permanent shift in how nations approach energy security and infrastructure investment. The IEA has underlined a four-decade high in nuclear power construction alongside the broader $3.4 trillion investment wave, accelerating the race toward grids, efficiency, and storage. Birol is convinced the Hormuz crisis is leading governments to rethink energy priorities and to seek to diversify partners, trade routes, fuels, and technologies. Given that the global energy crisis will continue to cast a long shadow into 2027, based on IEA leadership’s take on the situation, lingering supply bottlenecks and fractured trade routes are locking in a high-alert era for global energy security. Back in May 2026, the IEA’s ‘ World Energy Investment’ report outlined that the conflict in the Middle East was expected to make energy security a top priority among decision-makers, as its effects were being felt most directly in the Middle East and Asia, which had been the destination for 80-90% of energy exports from Gulf producers. The International Energy Agency said at the time that the conflict was fortifying a shift towards security, trust, and diversity as key considerations when choosing energy projects and partners, alongside costs, prices, and environmental performance. As a result, the IEA anticipated wide-ranging implications for the fuels and technologies that countries prioritize, where they get them from, and how they look to achieve other strategic energy objectives. " Changing perceptions of risk and reliability are expected to spur renewed interest in a range of domestically available energy resources: for key fuel importers, this creates upside for renewables, nuclear and potentially also for coal. Renewable energy resources are widely distributed around the world, and preliminary signs indicate that deployment is picking up in some markets heavily affected by the energy crisis. Moreover, if it prompts a faster pace of electrification, the conflict will bring the Age of Electricity even more clearly into view: electricity-related spending already makes up nearly 60% of all global energy investment. " — The International Energy Agency Related Articles Fossil Energy IEA: Oil & gas decline rates sound the alarm over global energy security risks 5 min read The Paris-based agency’s projections indicated that capital flows to the energy sector were expected to grow to $3.4 trillion in 2026, a 5% rise from 2025, mainly from China, the U.S., and the EU, with the clean energy investment set to grow to $2.2 trillion, almost double that of fossil fuels, as investment in clean energy increases year-on-year by 7% in advanced economies and in China, and 4% in other emerging markets, reflecting regional differences with a shared focus on energy security. The IEA has noted that geopolitical tensions, supply restrictions, and market shocks are impacting the outlook looking into 2027, stressing persistent risks to energy security and fuel supplies, alongside surging costs and heightened demand for power infrastructure resilience, energy storage, and nuclear build-outs, which have hit multi-decade highs with roughly 90 GW under construction. The total energy spending in the U.S. is set to rise by 6%, reaching almost $610 billion, with a nearly fourfold uptick in LNG spending in 2026, and battery storage, geothermal, and nuclear power emerging as investment drivers. The United States is expected to represent nearly half of global LNG export capacity by 2030. The investment in the Latin American region is anticipated to increase to $190 billion in 2026, with fossil fuel supply spending continuing to rise, led by deepwater oil developments in Brazil and Guyana and continued activity in Argentina, Mexico, and Venezuela, and grids remaining a focus sector. Advertisement Energy investments in the European Union are projected to rise to $440 billion in response to energy security and affordability concerns, supported by diversification and accelerated electrification, with natural gas investment remaining important for security of supply, especially through LNG, with infrastructure investments reaching $17 billion in 2025. Africa’s energy spending is forecast to reach $110 billion in 2026, dominated by fossil fuel spending, with growing interest in power generation, critical minerals, and transport, while upstream investment hit $37 billion in 2025, down from $68 billion in 2016, an 11% drop. Investment remains highly concentrated in Algeria, Angola, Egypt, Nigeria, and Libya, which together account for 70% of investment, even though investment in these countries has fallen from $50 billion in 2016 to $25 billion in 2025. On the other hand, capital allocated to emerging producers such as Mozambique, Namibia, Senegal, and Uganda has grown since 2016. The Middle East is continuing to attract energy investment, with natural gas and low-emissions technologies driving investment trends, but upstream oil and gas spending is projected to decline by around 1% in 2026. Eurasia continues to keep fossil fuels as the primary energy source in the region, while investment in renewables, grids, and electrification is projected to reach $43 billion. While total energy spending remains dominated by oil and gas, at $77 billion, regional fossil fuel investment has fallen markedly from past highs. There is a growing focus on power system reliability, grid expansion, and export resilience in countries such as Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan, which includes major public and foreign-backed projects in solar, wind, storage, hydropower and transmission infrastructure. China’s energy investment priorities are shifting from capacity expansion toward broader system strategy, with grid expansion and green finance underpinning energy transition, based on the IEA’s report. The country’s spending is forecast to hit $945 billion in 2026, with grid investment expected to rise sharply to $140 billion, playing a central role in integrating recent renewable additions, supporting electrification, and strengthening energy security. India’s energy investment is projected to climb to $170 billion, driven by a surge in investment in solar PV and oil refining, as for every dollar invested in fossil-based generation, the country invests three in renewables and nuclear power. Japan and Korea’s investment in dispatchable generation is becoming increasingly important for electricity security, while the region is expanding critical mineral investments to reduce supply chain risks by combining transition-related spending with a strong focus on energy security, with total investment projected to reach $122 billion. Southeast Asia’s energy investment continues to grow, with spending on renewables, grids, and end-use sectors anticipated to jump to $57 billion in 2026, as the region’s electricity demand is increasing 1.5 times faster than the global average, with the momentum building for cross-border electricity trade through the ASEAN Power Grid (APG), with $27 billion needed for cross-border interconnections by 2040. articles.title: Panama Canal to Name Terminal Bidders as Expansion Plans Advance
articles.summary: The Panama Canal expects to announce the pre-qualified bidders for a project to build and operate two new container terminals by the end of this year, Administrator Ilya Espino said on Wednesday, advancing a tender process linked to one of the…
articles.body: Panama Canal to Name Terminal Bidders as Expansion Plans Advance Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 (Credit: The Panama Canal) The Panama Canal expects to announce the pre-qualified bidders for a project to build and operate two new container terminals by the end of this year, Administrator Ilya Espino said on Wednesday, advancing a tender process linked to one of the world's most strategic trade corridors. Speaking at the Houston International Maritime Conference, Espino said the canal authority has evaluated initial proposals, and the shortlisted companies will next receive a request for proposals, moving the project into a more formal bidding stage. Espino did not elaborate on the pre-qualified companies but said that global shipping heavyweights such as Maersk and MSC, which already operate ports in Panama, could be potential bidders. The new terminals are part of a broader $8.5 billion expansion plan aimed at turning the Panama Canal into a larger logistics and energy hub beyond its role as a shipping passage, one of the world's most important arteries for maritime trade. That broader plan includes a proposed $4 billion to $8 billion pipeline to transport liquefied petroleum gas, as well as two new container terminals expected to attract another $2.6 billion in investment. Existing trans-shipment capacity in Panama is already tight, underpinning the push for expansion. Espino said the canal is also beginning to plan a third terminal project. Under the current timetable, concessions could be awarded around mid-2027, with operations starting in 2030 or 2031. Companies that showed early interest in the expansion projects include ENEOS, Energy Transfer, Exxon Mobil, Enterprise Products Partners, Chevron, Phillips, Targa Resources and ONEOK, the canal has said. Transit Demand The freshwater-operated canal has implemented some draft and passage restrictions this year in anticipation of a very strong El Niño weather pattern, which typically reduces rainfall in Panama. Espino said the highest amount paid this year by a ship to secure a Panama Canal transit reached $5.2 million, adding that the waterway continues to implement options to avoid long waiting times that can lead to high passage costs. The canal has recently introduced changes to its booking and auction systems as it tries to balance demand across vessel segments while protecting water resources. "We're hoping the worst we go in the dry season is 32 (vessels authorized per day), as far as slots. People value more spaces than draft, when you have to balance between one and the other, because then more clients have opportunity to make a reservation," she added. The current passage limit is 33 ships per day. Maximum authorized vessel draft could be adjusted in coming months depending on rainfall, Espino said. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) vessel traffic remains below typical levels amid ship reroutings. The canal is now seeing about three LNG vessels per week, but that is still below the two LNG ships per day that transited the canal before Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Espino said. "We have been very resilient in a very volatile world," she said. Due to the Ukraine-Russia war, the LNG market "disappeared from the canal" and is now starting to come back, Espino added. The waterway is expecting 10,750 deep-draft transits this fiscal year, which will end in September 2027, below the 12,636 transits of the previous fiscal year, according to Espino. (Reuters - Reporting by Marianna Parraga; Editing by Kylie Madry, Daina Beth Solomon and Jonathan Spicer)
