Photo courtesy Maersk/APM Terminals By Christian Wienberg and Sanne Wass Nov 5, 2026 (Bloomberg) –AP Moller-Maersk A/S shares slumped after a guidance upgrade and third-quarter earnings from the world’s second-largest shipping line fell short of analyst estimates. Maersk stock dropped as much as 11.6%, the most since April 2025, at 9:33 a.m. in Copenhagen. Shares are falling for the sixth day in a row, but are still up about 36% this year. Maersk now expects 2026 underlying earnings before interest and tax to be in a range of $8 billion to $8.5 billion, according to a statement on Thursday. The full range is below the average analyst estimate of $8.66 billion compiled by Bloomberg. Third-quarter Ebit, while up 155% from a year earlier at $3.27 billion, missed the $3.61 billion estimate. Revenue and Ebitda also came below estimates. “Maersk delivered third-quarter earnings that came in below expectations,” Mikkel Emil Jensen, an analyst at AL Sydbank, said in a note. “The main explanation lies in the Ocean business, where volume growth was slightly weaker than expected while costs came in higher than anticipated.” He listed lower activity in the Middle East and challenging weather conditions as some of the reasons for lower volumes. Still, Maersk’s new guidance compares with the Copenhagen-based company’s previous forecast range of $4.5 billion to $6.5 billion and is the second upgrade in just three months as a global rollout of artificial intelligence infrastructure boosts the demand and rates for shipping services. Chief Executive Officer Vincent Clerc told reporters in Copenhagen that “some analysts need to look into the spreadsheets.” Haider Anjum, a senior analyst at Jyske Bank, called the earnings strong but “not strong enough.” He said earnings continue to be driven by capacity disruptions around Hormuz, typhoons and port congestion, raising questions about how long those tailwinds can last. Repeated disruptions to global supply chains have boosted freight rates in recent years. They include the Covid-19 pandemic, Houthi attacks that forced carriers to avoid the Red Sea and most recently the US war against Iran that throttled traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. “The guidance also implies that fourth-quarter earnings will be slightly lower than in the third quarter, which is broadly in line with our expectations,” Jensen of AL Sydbank said. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Maersk raises 2026 guidance as Ocean earnings surge in third quarter
articles.summary: Maersk has raised its full-year 2026 earnings guidance following a strong third quarter, driven by higher ocean freight rates and continued supply chain disruptions that limited available shipping capacity. The Danish shipping group reported revenue of US$18.1 billion, up 27% from US$14.2 billion in the same period...
articles.body: Maersk has raised its full-year 2026 earnings guidance following a strong third quarter, driven by higher ocean freight rates and continued supply chain disruptions that limited available shipping capacity. The Danish shipping group reported revenue of US$18.1 billion, up 27% from US$14.2 billion in the same period last year. EBITDA increased to US$4.7 billion from US$2.7 billion, while EBIT rose to US$3.3 billion from US$1.3 billion. Net profit also increased to approximately US$3 billion, compared with US$1.1 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Following these results, Maersk increased its full-year underlying EBITDA forecast to US$14–14.5 billion, from its previous range of US$10.5–12.5 billion. The company also raised its underlying EBIT guidance to US$8–8.5 billion, compared with the previous forecast of US$4.5–6.5 billion. Meanwhile, expected free cash flow increased to more than US$3 billion. The revised outlook assumes global container market volume growth of approximately 4% for the full year. Higher freight rates drive Ocean earnings Maersk’s Ocean division accounted for most of the improvement in quarterly earnings. Ocean revenue increased by 37% to US$12.6 billion, while EBIT reached US$2.6 billion, compared with US$567 million a year earlier. The average loaded freight rate rose by approximately 46% year on year to US$3,287 per forty-foot equivalent unit (FFE). However, loaded container volumes declined by 0.8% to 3.37 million FFE. Despite the slight decrease, vessel utilisation remained high at 96%. The increase in freight rates was supported by capacity constraints across global shipping networks. Severe typhoons in East Asia caused significant port congestion, while the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted cargo flows and increased operating costs. According to Maersk, average global port waiting times reached 16.6 hours at their peak in August, the highest level since January 2023. Meanwhile, the Shanghai Containerised Freight Index increased by 46% during the third quarter compared with the previous quarter. Higher fuel prices also affected operating costs. Maersk’s average bunker price increased by 49% year on year, although bunker consumption declined by 6.3%, partly supported by the partial return to the Suez Canal. Vincent Clerc, Chief Executive Officer of Maersk, said global trade remained resilient despite geopolitical uncertainty and continued supply chain disruptions. He also highlighted growing demand linked to electrification, energy investment and the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Logistics and terminal operations support growth Maersk’s Logistics & Services division reported revenue of US$4.5 billion, an increase of 13% year on year. The division’s EBIT rose to US$259 million from US$218 million, while its EBIT margin improved to 5.8% from 5.5%. Growth was particularly strong in landside logistics, supported by landbridge operations across the Gulf region. Air freight, project logistics and contract logistics also contributed to higher revenue. Meanwhile, the Terminals division recorded its highest quarterly revenue, reaching US$1.52 billion. Terminal volumes increased by 2.6%, supported by growth in Africa and Europe of 14% and 6.7%, respectively. However, Terminals EBIT declined to US$493 million from US$571 million a year earlier. The comparison was affected by an impairment reversal recognised in 2025. Excluding that effect, EBIT increased by 6.5%. Maersk advances fleet and terminal investments Alongside its financial performance, Maersk continued investing in vessel capacity and port infrastructure. As part of its fleet renewal programme, the carrier ordered 26 dual-fuel containerships, each with a capacity of 18,600 TEU. Deliveries are scheduled for 2029 and 2030. In Bangladesh, APM Terminals began construction of the Laldia terminal in Chattogram during August. The project is expected to add 900,000 TEU of annual handling capacity. Meanwhile, APM Terminals Suape commenced commercial operations in Brazil in September. The new facility will initially provide up to 400,000 TEU of annual capacity. For the first nine months of 2026, Maersk generated revenue of US$46.8 billion, compared with US$40.7 billion during the corresponding period of 2025. Looking ahead, the company expects resilient container demand to support its upgraded financial outlook. However, geopolitical developments, freight rates and fuel costs remain important sources of uncertainty.

articles.title: ZIM’s ZX3 enters a Transpacific premium race already shaped by speed and landside access
articles.summary: ZIM’s planned ZX3 service between China and Los Angeles adds another competitor to the premium Transpacific market. But the significance of the launch extends beyond the advertised 12-day crossing from Shanghai. It places ZIM in competition with carriers that have already built expedited shipping products around...
articles.body: ZIM’s planned ZX3 service between China and Los Angeles adds another competitor to the premium Transpacific market. But the significance of the launch extends beyond the advertised 12-day crossing from Shanghai. It places ZIM in competition with carriers that have already built expedited shipping products around terminal operations, chassis availability and faster access to inland transport. The new service, announced by ZIM , is scheduled to begin in December 2026. As Container News reported , ZX3 will connect Xiamen and Shanghai directly with Los Angeles, joining the carrier’s existing ZEX and ZX2 expedited services. The competitive question is not whether ZIM can advertise a fast crossing. It is whether the new service can translate that speed into reliable cargo availability and efficient onward delivery in a market where rivals already offer comparable features. Ocean transit is only part of the comparison ZIM is advertising a 12-day Shanghai–Los Angeles transit and a 15-day connection from Xiamen. Both are scheduled service propositions rather than demonstrated operating results, as ZX3 has yet to begin. The wider market provides useful context, although published transit figures require careful interpretation. CMA CGM’s Eagle Express X (EXX) is marketed as an expedited Transpacific service linking Shanghai with Los Angeles. Its offering places emphasis on fast ocean transit and coordinated terminal operations, although advertised transit times should be distinguished from the carrier’s current sailing schedules and actual voyage performance. Matson’s published CLX service information lists a 10-day Shanghai–Long Beach ocean transit, with cargo availability the following day. The destination is Long Beach rather than Los Angeles, making it relevant to competition across the Southern California gateway without representing an identical port-to-port comparison. These distinctions matter because a carrier’s advertised crossing time does not necessarily reflect its current schedule, actual voyage performance or the time at which an importer can collect cargo. Consequently, ZX3’s 12-day offering should be assessed as part of a competitive expedited product, not as evidence that ZIM will operate the fastest service in the market. The terminal is becoming part of the product The most revealing aspect of ZX3 is its destination-side operating model. ZIM plans to use a dedicated berth at West Basin Container Terminal in Los Angeles, supported by a dedicated container yard, pickup lanes and chassis arrangements. The carrier also advertises Monday arrivals and expedited cargo availability without appointments or queues. These features are commercially important because the benefit of a fast ocean crossing can be diminished by delays between vessel arrival, discharge and cargo collection. Yet ZIM is not alone in offering such arrangements. CMA CGM’s EXX product uses Fenix Marine Services in Los Angeles and advertises dedicated chassis, a container yard for expedited pickup and coordinated cargo handling. Its commercial proposition combines ocean speed with predictable terminal operations. Matson similarly promotes dedicated terminal facilities at Long Beach, next-day cargo availability and an off-dock operation designed to facilitate faster truck collections. The common feature is the integration of terminal access into the shipping product. Rather than treating discharge as the end of the ocean carrier’s competitive proposition, these services place greater emphasis on what happens immediately after the vessel arrives. ZX3 therefore represents an expansion of ZIM’s participation in an established form of premium competition, rather than the introduction of an entirely new operating concept. Inland connections extend the competitive field The same pattern is visible in inland transport. ZIM says ZX3 will provide expedited rail connections to destinations including Chicago, New York, Memphis, Dallas and Kansas City. This extends the service proposition beyond importers collecting containers in Southern California. CMA CGM promotes its EXX RailFlash offering, including rail connections from Los Angeles to major inland markets. Matson also markets expedited intermodal services through its logistics operations. For shippers, these arrangements can be as important as the ocean crossing itself. A container that arrives quickly at the West Coast but misses an inland connection may lose much of its time advantage. However, the available announcements do not establish which carrier offers the fastest end-to-end transit to individual inland destinations. Such a comparison would require matching origin points, vessel schedules, discharge times, rail departures and cargo availability at the final destination. It would also need to account for differences between advertised services and actual performance. Without those measurements, no reliable ranking of ZX3, EXX and CLX/MAX can be established across the full supply chain. What ZX3 adds to ZIM’s network Beyond individual transit times, ZX3 expands the geographical coverage and frequency of ZIM’s expedited offering. The company says the addition will bring its premium network, including ZEX and ZX2, to seven weekly departures from China and Vietnam to the US West Coast. This is relevant because premium service competition also depends on sailing frequency and the availability of alternative departures. More weekly options may help customers manage shipment timing, although the number of departures does not by itself establish capacity, reliability or market share. Xiamen is another important element. ZIM is positioning ZX3 as a dedicated premium offering for that origin, alongside an additional direct Shanghai connection. The commercial significance will depend on how much cargo the service attracts, whether its schedules perform consistently and how effectively the terminal and inland arrangements operate after launch. ZIM has not provided sufficient public operating data to quantify those outcomes. The real test begins after launch The competitive implications of ZX3 will become clearer once the service enters operation in December. Several measures will matter: actual Shanghai and Xiamen transit times, consistency of Monday arrivals, the interval between berthing and cargo availability, and the performance of inland connections. Those results will determine whether ZIM can deliver a commercially meaningful alternative to established expedited offerings. For now, the launch demonstrates that premium Transpacific competition increasingly encompasses the full journey from Asian loading port to US cargo collection and inland distribution. ZIM’s challenge is not simply to cross the Pacific quickly. It is to deliver the coordinated terminal and inland performance that customers increasingly expect from an expedited shipping product.
takeaways: ZIM’s planned ZX3 service between China and Los Angeles adds another competitor to the premium Transpacific market.
But the significance of the launch extends beyond the advertised 12-day crossing from Shanghai.
It places ZIM in competition with carriers that have already built expedited shipping products around terminal operations, chassis availability and faster access to inland transport.

articles.body: Business & Finance November 5, 2026 · 19 minutes ago Saipem7 closing in on its debut as Brazil clears Saipem-Subsea7 merger The multibillion-dollar merger between Saipem and Subsea7 has secured Brazil’s blessing, pending divestment of a vessel. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Saipem Italy’s engineering, drilling, and construction services giant Saipem and the Luxembourg-domiciled Subsea7 have made inroads in bringing their proposed business combination closer to completion, with the green light from Brazil’s antitrust watchdog, the Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (CADE), clearing a major regulatory hurdle while conditioning the approval on the sale of a pipelaying vessel to preserve market competition. Saipem and Subsea7 have received the approval from Brazil’s CADE for their proposed combination to create Saipem7, subject to compliance with the commitments set out in a merger control agreement. The duo has committed to divest the Seven Borealis vessel to address the competition concerns raised by CADE’s tribunal during its review. This commitment includes specific provisions to ensure continuity in the execution of the existing project backlog. Both companies have emphasized that the divestiture is not expected to materially affect the strategic rationale of the proposed combination. As a result, they have confirmed the synergies previously announced. The European players underlined: “Subsea7 and Saipem remain firmly committed to the proposed combination and will continue to work constructively with the relevant authorities to secure prompt satisfaction (or, where applicable, waiver) of the remaining conditions set out in the common merger plan approved by the shareholders of both companies.” This go-ahead in Brazil comes after Saipem and Subsea7 announced the end of the U.S. antitrust review period, giving them the all-clear to close the transaction in America. The duo’s merger is not out of the woods yet, as the conclusion of the European Commission’s in-depth investigation to assess the proposed merger is still ongoing. articles.body: Expeditors International reported strong third-quarter results, supported by higher ocean and airfreight volumes and continued demand for customs and logistics services. Revenue increased by 42% year on year to US$4.1 billion. Operating income rose by 55% to US$445 million, while net earnings attributable to shareholders climbed by 55% to US$345 million. Diluted earnings per share reached US$2.65, representing an increase of 62% from the third quarter of 2025. Expeditors returned US$197 million to shareholders through share repurchases during the quarter. Dividends and repurchases totalled US$946 million during the first nine months of 2026. Ocean container volumes rise 7% Ocean container volumes increased by 7% year on year during the quarter. The company recorded particularly strong growth in September and across Asian export markets. Expeditors said container demand remained healthy despite congestion at major Asian ports and transshipment hubs. Three consecutive typhoons disrupted port operations, idled capacity and affected vessel schedules. The logistics company used its carrier relationships to secure capacity and maintain services during the disruptions. It expects port congestion and wider supply chain challenges to continue through the remainder of 2026. Airfreight tonnage increased by 13%, reaching a quarterly record. Growth was led by South Asian exports and demand from hyperscalers and suppliers supporting artificial intelligence infrastructure. Air cargo capacity remained constrained by limited fleet growth and delays in new aircraft deliveries. Expeditors said demand continued to outpace available capacity, keeping freight rates elevated. Customs and logistics services expand Customs brokerage, Transcon road freight, distribution and order management each achieved double-digit revenue growth for a third consecutive quarter. The company attributed the improvement to new customer wins, higher customs declaration volumes and demand from technology companies. “We continue to gain share, particularly in markets that we have made a strategic focus,” said Daniel Wall, President and Chief Executive Officer of Expeditors. Wall added that the company’s focus on expanding its customer base and diversifying revenue was supporting more durable performance across different operating conditions. Chief Financial Officer David Hackett said revenue grew by 42% while headcount increased by only 1%. Expeditors’ operating efficiency reached 36.7%, above its historical target of 30%. The company continues to invest in temperature-controlled facilities, critical logistics services, artificial intelligence and other technology solutions. Expeditors will hold an Investor Day for shareholders and analysts in New York on 18 November 2026.

Join the leading maritime news network Improving vessel energy efficiency is an important part of the maritime industry’s efforts to reduce fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. While hull performance often receives significant attention, the condition of a vessel’s propeller also plays an important role in maintaining propulsion efficiency throughout its operating cycle. Propspeed has joined RightShip’s Zero Harm Innovation Partners Program, bringing its expertise in biocide-free, foul-release propeller coatings to a collaborative network focused on advancing safer and more sustainable maritime operations. Through the Program, Propspeed aims to raise awareness of the role propeller surface condition plays in vessel performance and how coating technologies can help shipowners and managers manage efficiency losses associated with biofouling and propeller surface condition. A vessel’s propulsion efficiency depends on several factors, including the condition of its hull and propeller surfaces. Over time, operational wear, marine growth, corrosion, cavitation erosion and mechanical damage can increase surface roughness, affecting the flow of water across propeller blades. As surface roughness increases, more power may be required to maintain vessel speed, contributing to higher fuel consumption, operating costs and associated emissions. Although propellers account for a relatively small proportion of a vessel’s total wetted surface area, fouling on these surfaces can have a disproportionately large effect on propulsion efficiency. The extent of deterioration depends on factors such as vessel operating conditions, trading patterns, ports of call and periods spent idle. Managing propeller surface condition is therefore an important consideration in maintaining vessel performance between scheduled dry dockings. Propspeed has developed a biocide-free coating system specifically designed for propeller surfaces, helping protect propeller efficiency by reducing surface roughness, while also limiting the accumulation of marine growth and its impact on performance. The system consists of two components: an etching primer that bonds to the metal substrate and a silicone-based foul-release topcoat. Together, they create an ultra-smooth, hydrophobic surface that helps reduce propeller surface roughness and makes it more difficult for marine organisms to adhere. Applied during scheduled dry docking, the coating is designed to help preserve propeller surface condition as vessels return to service and throughout their operating cycle. This approach addresses a particular challenge in marine coating applications. Propellers operate in demanding environments, where coatings must withstand mechanical and operational stresses while maintaining adhesion and foul-release properties. By helping reduce surface roughness from day of application and limiting additional roughness caused by biofouling, Propspeed’s technology aims to support more consistent propulsion efficiency between dockings. Maintaining propeller efficiency has implications beyond vessel performance. By reducing the additional power demand associated with increased surface roughness, effective propeller maintenance can contribute to lower fuel consumption and associated greenhouse gas emissions. Propspeed’s approach also considers the environmental implications of biofouling management. Its coating system does not rely on biocides to discourage marine growth. Instead, the silicone-based surface is designed to make it harder for organisms to attach, supporting biofouling management while potentially reducing the risk of transferring invasive aquatic species between marine environments. The foul-release properties may also reduce the need for repeated underwater propeller polishing during a coating’s service life. Where this reduces the frequency of diving interventions, it could help limit associated costs and occupational safety exposure. These potential benefits illustrate how attention to a specific component of vessel performance can contribute to broader operational and sustainability objectives. Actual efficiency improvements and fuel savings will depend on vessel-specific conditions and operating practices. Propspeed’s participation in RightShip’s Zero Harm Innovation Partners Program reflects a shared interest in practical technologies that can contribute to safer and more sustainable maritime operations. Through the Program, Propspeed aims to encourage greater industry awareness of propeller efficiency and its contribution to vessel energy performance. This includes promoting a more considered approach to propeller maintenance alongside other vessel efficiency measures. RightShip’s Zero Harm Innovation Partners Program brings together organisations across the maritime supply chain to encourage the development and adoption of technologies and solutions that support the industry’s journey towards Zero Harm. By fostering knowledge sharing and long-term collaboration, the Program aims to support coordinated progress on safety and sustainability challenges. As part of this network, Propspeed brings a focused approach to managing propeller surface condition and its implications for vessel efficiency. RightShip looks forward to working with Propspeed to encourage knowledge exchange and greater awareness of practical approaches that can support more efficient and environmentally responsible maritime operations. articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard is exploring the use of commercial icebreaking vessels to help keep Northeast ports and waterways open this winter, as the service prepares for another season of...

Join the leading maritime news network Coast Guard Cutter Penobscot Bay, a 140-foot bay-class icebreaking tug, breaks ice on the Hudson River in support of Operation Reliable Energy for Northeast Winters (OPRENEW), February 11, 2021. OPRENEW is the Coast Guard's effort to keep waterways clear of ice during the winter months. (U.S. Coast Guard photo illustration by Petty Officer 3rd Class Anthony Pappaly) The U.S. Coast Guard is exploring the use of commercial icebreaking vessels to help keep Northeast ports and waterways open this winter, as the service prepares for another season of potentially disruptive ice conditions. In an October 21 Request for Information (RFI) posted on SAM.gov, the Coast Guard is seeking U.S.-flag, Jones Act-qualified vessels capable of supporting emergency icebreaking operations across New England and southern Connecticut. The goal is to maintain commercial shipping channels, ensure deliveries of critical cargo, and reduce navigational risks during periods of heavy ice. The Coast Guard is looking for vessels capable of operating in ice ranging from 4 to 18 inches thick, with the ability to mobilize to the Northeast by January 2, 2027. Potential operating areas include Boston Harbor, the Cape Cod Canal, Buzzards Bay, Nantucket, Martha’s Vineyard, Narragansett Bay, and Connecticut ports including Bridgeport, Stamford, and New Haven. Under the proposed arrangement, commercial operators would provide the vessels, crews, equipment, and supervision, while the Coast Guard would direct operational priorities. The service anticipates providing 72 hours’ notice before operations, with a minimum seven-day operating window for continuous support. Vessels would be expected to work up to 12 hours per day during daylight hours, with longer operations requiring approval. The Coast Guard is also asking operators to describe their ability to clear shipping channels, maintain navigable tracks, escort vessels carrying critical cargo, and assist communities affected by ice jams or flooding. Only U.S.-flag, coastwise-qualified vessels will be considered. The request follows a difficult 2025–2026 winter that saw severe ice conditions across the Northeast and Great Lakes, forcing the Coast Guard to deploy icebreaking assets to maintain commercial navigation. In January, the Coast Guard launched Operation Reliable Energy for Northeast Winters (RENEW), emphasizing the importance of keeping heating oil and other essential supplies moving through the region’s waterways. At the time, the service acknowledged that some icebreaking assets were undergoing maintenance and upgrades, requiring operational adjustments to concentrate resources where they were most needed. The new commercial vessel initiative also comes as the Coast Guard moves forward with plans to modernize its aging domestic icebreaking fleet. The service is pursuing the acquisition of up to seven Homeland Security Cutter–Light Icebreakers to replace its aging 65-foot icebreaking tugs, which perform critical winter missions throughout the Northeast. The Coast Guard issued a formal solicitation for the new vessels earlier this year, with final proposals due in October. The commercial icebreaking request could provide another option for meeting near-term winter demands while that modernization effort moves forward. For now, the Coast Guard is conducting market research rather than soliciting binding bids. The agency is requesting information on vessel capabilities, previous icebreaking experience, mobilization timelines, operating limitations, and potential contract structures. Operators may also submit preliminary pricing information, including daily rates and mobilization costs. The RFI does not specify how many commercial vessels may ultimately be needed or the potential value of a future contract. Responses are due November 13, 2026, at 5 p.m. Eastern. The Coast Guard emphasized that the notice is for planning purposes only and does not guarantee a future solicitation or contract award. articles.summary: On October 29, 2026, a Somali Pirate Action Group of 12 armed pirates hijacked the Iranian fishing dhow AZINI approximately 185 nautical miles east of Bandarbeyla, Puntland. The vessel’s crew reportedly included 21 Iranian fishermen and two Somali security guards.On November 2…

November 4, 2026 Fishing vessels targeted by Somali pirates in 2026, as of November 2. Positions are approximate except AZINI’s reported hijack position. The LIAO DONG YU 578 capture has not been officially confirmed, and the unnamed dhow (05) is a possible hijack with no reported position, plotted off its destination. Source: Windward Maritime AI Platform. On October 29, 2026, a Somali Pirate Action Group of 12 armed pirates hijacked the Iranian fishing dhow AZINI approximately 185 nautical miles east of Bandarbeyla, Puntland. The vessel’s crew reportedly included 21 Iranian fishermen and two Somali security guards. On November 2, the Indian Navy freed the vessel following a 48-hour operation in the Arabian Sea, and all crew are reportedly safe. The hijacking of AZINI is the first confirmed hijacking of the fourth quarter and the fourth confirmed hijacking of a dhow or fishing vessel off Somalia this year. It follows a string of seizures that peaked in the spring. On January 1, the China-flagged LIAO DONG YU 578 (MMSI 412549025) was reportedly captured by pirates off Bandarbeyla while fishing, although official sources have not confirmed the hijacking. The Chinese Embassy in Somalia reported that a Chinese fishing vessel was released from pirate custody on March 2, but did not name the vessel. On March 24, a PAG seized the Iran-flagged fishing dhow ALWASEEMI 786 , which was abandoned under naval pressure on April 5. The fishing vessel ALKHARY 2 was hijacked on approximately April 20 and released on April 22. On April 25, a PAG seized the UAE-flagged dhow FAHAD 4 and reportedly used it as a mothership in an attempted attack on the MINERVA PISCES on April 28. The pirates then abandoned the dhow in the Arabian Sea on May 4 after their supplies ran short. An unnamed dhow was reportedly hijacked on May 9 while en route to Kismayo, and its current status is unknown. At least two unnamed Iranian dhows were also reportedly seized and released after a $40,000 ransom payment, although official sources have not confirmed these incidents. Why Attacks on Dhows Go Underreported Attacks on dhows and fishing vessels by PAGs off Somalia are likely underreported. Many of the Iranian dhows fishing in the region are part of an unregulated fleet that does not broadcast IMO numbers and frequently operates with AIS off, a practice that may also serve as a defensive measure against piracy. These vessels are also low-value targets. They command far smaller ransoms than merchant vessels, so their seizures draw less attention than attacks on commercial shipping. The confirmed count is very likely a floor rather than a full picture. Why Pirates Target Fishing Vessels Pirates are likely targeting fishing vessels for two reasons. Motherships Extend Pirate Range Toward Shipping Lanes Dhows and fishing vessels can be used as motherships that extend the range of PAGs far offshore and toward major shipping lanes. The Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO) highlighted this risk following the AZINI hijacking. The FAHAD 4 case shows the threat in practice, since pirates used the dhow to attempt an attack on a merchant vessel three days after seizing it. Resentment Over Illegal Fishing Illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing by foreign fleets is a documented driver of attacks on fishing vessels. Pirates involved in the seizure of foreign fishing vessels have cited resentment against illegal fishers as the reason for their attacks.

articles.body: Oil Prices Drop 9% After Republicans Lose Congress in Midterm Elections Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Piya W. Oil prices fell 9% on Wednesday in volatile trading as investors awaited Washington's next move in the US-Israeli war with Iran after President Donald Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress in midterm elections. Brent futures dropped $9.27, or 8.9%, to $94.29 a barrel, touching the lowest level since September 4, at 11:58 a.m. ET (1658 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $7.44, or 7.8%, to $88.54. Brent settled in the previous session at its lowest level in nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to end wars in Ukraine and Iran. "Larger crude oil exports out of the Middle East, along with President Trump stating he has no immediate plans to strike Iran, is keeping the pressure on crude oil prices for now. The Democratic control of Congress could also tighten US military spending in the Middle East and further heighten the possibility of a peace deal sooner than later," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at US financial services firm BOK Financial. Trump acknowledged that the Iran war had played a role in his party's sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, as Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that the United States had no immediate plans to strike Iran. Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement that US hostility would persist regardless of which party was in power. Yemen's Houthis said they had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. There was no confirmation from Saudi authorities. "The elections are giving bears a reason to cast doubt on a continuation in Iran ... Gulf exports of crude, condensate and refined products, excluding liquefied petroleum gas, averaged 17.1 million barrels per day in October, according to ship-tracking data from Vortexa, down from 18.9 million bpd in September but still roughly three-quarters of pre-war levels. In the US, crude stocks, gasoline and distillate inventories fell last week, the Energy Information Administration said. Crude inventories fell by 865,000 barrels to 409.8 million barrels in the week ended October 30, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for an 877,000-barrel rise. Photo: Department of War The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a network of individuals and companies accused of operating fraudulent ship registries that helped Iran’s shadow fleet evade sanctions, while issuing a new warning to maritime companies about the risks of dealing with falsely flagged vessels. The U.S. Treasury Department announced the sanctions on Wednesday as part of Operation Economic Outcast, targeting an India-based network led by Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid. According to Treasury, the couple operated a network of fraudulent flag registries and maritime certification services that allowed sanctioned tankers carrying Iranian petroleum to continue operating under flags they were not legally authorized to fly. Some of those vessels were transporting oil on behalf of Iran’s military and its proxies, Treasury said. The network allegedly impersonated maritime authorities in countries including Guyana, Eswatini, Laos, Aruba, Nicaragua, and Sint Maarten, issuing registration documents and certifications without authorization from the governments involved. In many cases, the operation relied on websites designed to look like legitimate national ship registries, offering everything from vessel registration to seafarer certification and classification services. Treasury said the scheme dates back to at least 2014, when Sharma and Shahid sought to impersonate the flag administration of Dominica. In 2023, Sharma established Singapore-based Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE Ltd., which continued providing registration services for vessels transporting Iranian oil even after authorities in Eswatini publicly disavowed the operation. Among the vessels identified by Treasury was the sanctioned tanker PING SHUN (IMO 9231901), which had previously transported multiple shipments of Iranian oil. The network also allegedly provided false flags to sanctioned tankers LATTAFA (IMO 9245794), BINARY STAR (IMO 9380570), and VERA (IMO 9304655). Treasury cited the case of the MAJESTIC X , formerly PHONIX (IMO 9198317), which was seized by U.S. military forces on April 22 while carrying Iranian oil. The tanker had been operating under a fraudulent Guyana flag. The sanctions target Sharma, Shahid, two associates, and nine companies and organizations linked to the network, including Oceaniek Technologies India, Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited, and Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry. OFAC Warns Maritime Industry Over False Flags Alongside the designations, the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new industry alert warning that companies providing services to vessels operating under fraudulent flags could face sanctions or penalties. The warning reflects a growing problem in the shadow fleet trade, where vessels increasingly rely on questionable or outright fraudulent registrations after being removed from legitimate flag registries. OFAC said that while shadow fleet operators have long used frequent flag changes to obscure their activities, fraudulent registries have become an increasingly common way to keep sanctioned vessels operating. These registries can create the appearance of legitimate registration even when the country whose flag is being used has never authorized the vessel to fly it. OFAC urged insurers, financial institutions, and other maritime service providers to conduct additional due diligence when dealing with vessels showing signs of false registration. Among the warning signs identified by OFAC are vessels with unknown flags, registration documents that cannot be verified, and discrepancies between a ship’s reported flag and the country code associated with its Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number. The agency also warned about vessels claiming flags from countries without recognized ship registries. The implications extend beyond sanctions compliance. Flag states are responsible for overseeing vessel safety, certification, and compliance with international maritime regulations. Vessels operating under fraudulent registrations may lack legitimate regulatory oversight and valid insurance coverage. Treasury warned that falsely flagged vessels could expose coastal nations to billions of dollars in potential environmental and economic damages in the event of a major maritime casualty. OFAC also encouraged governments to investigate fraudulent registries operating in their names and report suspected cases to the International Maritime Organization so that maritime databases accurately reflect vessels with invalid registrations. Broader Pressure on Iran The measures are part of Operation Economic Outcast, a sanctions campaign launched in August aimed at cutting off the financial networks supporting Iran’s oil exports and other economic activities. The latest action comes as the United States continues its maritime blockade of Iran amid the ongoing war, with Washington seeking to disrupt the networks that allow Iranian oil to reach international markets. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that companies and individuals continuing to support the Iranian government would face consequences. “We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air,” Bessent said. The sanctions package also included Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc., which Treasury said continued providing ground handling services to several sanctioned Iranian airlines. The maritime designations and new OFAC advisory highlight Washington’s growing focus on the service providers and intermediaries that keep Iran’s shadow fleet operating, rather than the tankers themselves. SAUL LOEB/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday blamed Republicans’ midterm election losses on the Trump administration’s eight-month war with Iran, which has driven up global energy prices and left commercial shipping under continued threat in the Strait of Hormuz. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote on X , a day after Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. Vance argued that the results reflected growing frustration with the war, rather than simply a failure by Republicans to turn out their voters. He cited internal polling showing four major concerns among voters: ending the Iran war, inflation and the cost of living, putting America first, and the United States’ relationship with Israel. The remarks are notable coming from the vice president of an administration that launched the war in February and has spent much of the year defending its military campaign. As recently as September, Vance resisted calling the conflict a war, telling reporters at a White House briefing that major combat operations had already ended. “I wouldn’t call it a war,” he said at the time. Vance also said Washington would not return to negotiations with Tehran until Iran stopped attacking commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. President Donald Trump has also acknowledged that the war contributed to Republicans’ election losses, although he defended his decision to launch the military campaign. “I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” Trump told The Wall Street Journal. The comments come as the administration faces growing pressure over the war’s economic consequences, including higher fuel prices and continued disruptions to global shipping. The war, launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, has left the Strait of Hormuz at the center of a prolonged military and economic standoff. The United States has maintained a blockade targeting Iranian maritime commerce, while Iran has continued attacking merchant ships in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf. Although tanker traffic has recovered considerably from the early months of the conflict, the security situation remains volatile. Several new maritime incidents were reported over the weekend, including attacks on tankers and other commercial vessels. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued additional warnings this week, highlighting the continued danger to merchant shipping despite U.S. efforts to secure the waterway. The disruption has driven up tanker rates, war-risk insurance costs, and global energy prices. Brent crude has remained above $100 a barrel, while higher gasoline and diesel prices have added to concerns about the cost of living in the United States. The election results now add another layer of uncertainty over the future of the conflict. With Democrats set to take control of Congress in January, the administration could face greater scrutiny of its military strategy, the continued blockade of Iranian shipping, and the economic costs of the war. Congress controls defense spending and could pursue legislation seeking to limit military operations, although Trump would retain substantial executive authority and the ability to veto legislation. For the shipping industry, the immediate questions remain whether Washington will continue its current approach, resume major combat operations, or reach an agreement with Tehran that could reduce threats to commercial vessels. Vance’s remarks come as the White House weighs those options, with the vice president now publicly blaming the administration’s own war for Republicans’ loss of Congress.
